key_references: Du et al. 2023; Li et al. 2025; Agapiou et al. 2022
support_summary: Known multi-agent learning problem: unclear which agent caused an outcome; agents must generalise to unfamiliar co-players.

key_references: Hu et al. 2020; Treutlein et al. 2021; Emmons et al. 2022
support_summary: Zero- and few-shot coordination research: without shared history or communication, agents must coordinate blind.
Argued: AI cyber-offence and surveillance make threats cheaper, more widespread and harder to detect.

key_references: Foerster et al. 2016; Lazaridou & Baroni 2020; Sukhbaatar et al. 2016
support_summary: Emergent-communication research on constrained channels; strategic withholding expected to dominate as capabilities grow.
Formal results: private valuations make efficient bargaining impossible to guarantee and can lead to costly conflict.

key_references: Albert et al. 2000; Kunegis et al. 2013
support_summary: Network theory: AI-AI preferential attachment could centralise AI nodes or trigger phase transitions. Only anecdote cited (forum bots, Kulveit 2023).
Argued: many agents built on few foundation models share failure modes, vulnerabilities and biases.
Co-adaptation autocurricula: emergent tool use in hide-and-seek; agents learning manipulative communication.

key_references: Zinkevich et al. 2005; Paes Leme et al. 2024
support_summary: Formal results: multi-agent Q-learning can cycle; auto-bidding dynamics can fail to converge to truthful equilibria.
Formal results: chaotic learning dynamics become the norm as agent count grows; paper notes not yet seen in frontier AI.
Formal results: small parameter changes (e.g. RL exploration rate) cause bifurcations in equilibria.

key_references: Stastny et al. 2021; Papoudakis et al. 2019
support_summary: Argued: co-adapting agents create non-stationarity; narrow training co-players cause overconfidence in negotiation.
Argued: easily created, deceptive agents garner little trust, causing economic inefficiency and pressure to defect.
Hypothetical: composed narrow tools (e.g. automated chemistry workflow) exceed individual capabilities. CS12 gives partial lab evidence.
Hypothetical: engagement-optimising moderation bots collectively shift users' politics. Paper states no advanced-AI examples are known.
Extrapolated from non-AI bot swarms to adaptive AI agents that jointly find new attack surfaces.
Argued: many coordinated, seemingly independent agents persuade or phish more effectively and evade detection.

key_references: Motwani et al. 2024; Franzmeyer et al. 2023; Draguns et al. 2024
support_summary: Steganography, illusory attacks and encrypted backdoors shown to evade detection. Motwani et al. is also the CS5 source but is not cross-referenced here as a case study.

A false belief originating with one agent is adopted by others and acted on, so a group with a common objective coordinates on something untrue. Authored because Hammond's FM1 instances (Incompatible Strategies, Credit Assignment, Limited Interactions) do not cover belief contagion.

Agents cooperate, usually covertly, to subvert an evaluation, scorer or monitoring scheme. Authored because FM3's definition names oversight schemes but Table 1 instantiates only Markets and Steganography.
Agents copy peers' observed choices in place of their own assessment, so one agent's pick propagates through the group. Distinct from Error Propagation, which carries a falsity rather than a choice.
